newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Outlook seen bullish for Australian economy in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Outlook seen bullish for Australian economy in 1997.

text.p: Expectations that Australia's economy will continue to strengthen through 1997 were boosted on Tuesday by the release of two strong indicators of activity which also signal further interest rate cuts may not be needed.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported that retail sales rose 2.7 percent in January, the strongest monthly rise in almost three years, while building approvals jumped 10.4 percent to their highest level since May 1995.
The upbeat data, which came on the same day as the monthly policy setting meeting of the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), was welcomed by analysts and the government.

"The RBA Board met today with evidence that the housing sector is not only warming up but is hot and that, beyond reasonable doubt, the worst is behind in the retail sector," Citibank Australia economists said in a commentary.
The government was also keen to trumpet the signs of stronger economic growth, which should help lower unemployment from around 8.5 percent as the year progresses.

"(The data) shows that there is a growing and strengthening in the economy, which is consistent with the government's expectations that the economy will pick up over the course of 1997 and 1998," Treasurer Peter Costello told Parliament.
While economists broadly concurred, they did add the rider that the January data may have overstated the strength of the economy, just as December data had understated it.

The pickup in retail trade, the largest monthly rise since March 1994, reversed much of the weakness through the second half of 1996, and fitted in with signs of strengthening employment at the end of 1996 and into early 1997.
Building appprovals are also performing strongly, up 22.5 percent over the past year. Strength in housing is seen flowing through to further gains in employment and retail spending.

"Today's retail and dwelling figures are consistent with the view that there will be a significant pickup in growth over the course of this year, and with the view that the RBA has already done enough," Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said.
"Further rate cuts are off the agenda, but there is no reason to expect a rate rise anytime soon," he said.
All of this fits in nicely with the view that the RBA was expressing a couple of weeks ago.
Then, the bank said the effects of the three interest rate cuts in 1996 were starting to come through, and economic data were showing signs of firming activity.

"The outlook now is for stronger growth during 1997 than that experienced through 1996," the RBA said in its monthly Bulletin. Combined with some concerns about the wages outlook, this meant the RBA saw "current monetary policy settings as broadly appropriate for the time being."

But while the future was looking bright, analysts were paring back forecasts for December quarter gross domestic product (GDP) after weaker than expected exports data. The figures will be released on Wednesday.
The Bureau of Statistics said net exports will detract 1.0 percentage points from expenditure based GDP growth, compared to expectations of a detraction of around 0.3 points.
That in turn will see forecasts for the average measure of GDP pared back by around 0.2 percentage points for the quarter to around 0.4 to 0.5 percent, economists said.
However, the historical nature of the data means its impact is expected to be muted in the face of stronger growth in 1997.

"While the net exports data may pull fourth quarter growth down somewhat, the data are historical and unlikely to shift the RBA's view of the world much," Hambros Australia fixed income economist Su-Lin Ong said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1900
